Volume 12 · Chapter 04

Likelihood and nonlinear models

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c03

By the endEstimate nonlinear models and distinguish functional-form identification from causal identification.

Volume 12 · Chapter 4

Likelihood and nonlinear models

A credit analyst observes a repayment indicator, an insurer observes a claim count, and a researcher sees earnings only for people who work. The same least-squares recipe does not describe these observations. A likelihood starts by describing what is observed and how its probability or density depends on parameters. That can sharpen estimation, but a precise estimate from the wrong observation model answers the wrong question.

Capability. Derive likelihood scores and information; prove a bounded regular estimation result; fit and interpret binary and count models; account for both coefficient and population-distribution uncertainty in an average predictive effect; construct a selection likelihood; and recognize a moving-support model where regular information arguments fail. Every numerical law and sample here is an original teaching construction.

Prerequisites. Identification and asymptotic tools supplies the iid LLN/CLT, uniform finite-net argument, stochastic orders and delta method. Linear models and robust inference supplies projection and covariance reasoning. IV and GMM distinguishes identification, local rank and signed score expansions. We state the specific regularity conditions needed here. The chapter does not inherit a dependent-data, growing-dimension or post-selection inference theorem.

1. A density is an observation model

Let W be an observation and fθ(w) a density relative to a specified measure ν, with θ a k×1 parameter. For discrete W the measure may be counting measure; for continuous W it may be Lebesgue measure; selected data can require both. A density value is not the probability of one exact continuous observation. For iid W₁,…,Wₙ the likelihood is Lₙ(θ)=∏ᵢfθ(Wᵢ); its average log is Qₙ(θ)=n−1∑ᵢℓ(Wᵢ,θ), where ℓ=log f. Maximization compares candidate parameter values for the observed data.

A correct likelihood contains the true observation law fθ₀. A quasi-likelihood uses the same criterion even when that family is a working approximation. Its target, if unique, is θ*=argmaxθ∈ΘEPℓ(W,θ) under the actual law P. Calling a procedure maximum likelihood does not establish that θ* equals a desired structural or causal parameter.

KL identity and equality condition. Suppose all candidates are positive on a common support S, vanish outside S, integrate to one, and the relevant log ratios and expected log densities are integrable under fθ₀. With r=fθ/fθ₀, normalization gives Eθ₀r=1. Since log r≤r−1, with equality only when r=1,

Q(θ₀)−Q(θ)=Eθ₀log[fθ₀(W)/fθ(W)] = KL(fθ₀,fθ)≥0.

The nonnegative random variable r−1−log r has expectation equal to this difference. Equality therefore implies r=1 almost surely under fθ₀, and conversely identical densities give equality. Identification of the parameter requires the additional implication fθ=fθ₀ almost everywhere ⇒ θ=θ₀. Two labels for the same density are not distinguished by likelihood. If P is outside the family, maximizing expected log density instead selects the best approximation for this criterion; the information inequality does not turn that approximation into the truth.

For conditional models fβ(y|x), apply the same argument conditional on X and then average over its actual distribution. A nuisance marginal density of X that does not depend on β adds a parameter-free log term and can be omitted when estimating β. This is a statement about a statistical conditional distribution. Interpreting a change in x as an intervention requires additional causal assumptions. The scoped likelihood lectures develop the KL motivation; the proofs and qualifications here make the required claims explicit.

2. Score and information require a valid interchange

Define the k×1 score s(w,θ)=∂ℓ(w,θ)/∂θ and symmetric k×k Hessian H(w,θ)=∂²ℓ(w,θ)/∂θ∂θ′. A score is measured in reciprocal parameter units. Its covariance, and information when the identity below holds, is measured in products of reciprocal parameter units. Information for n independent identically distributed observations is n times the one-observation information.

Sufficient interchange conditions. In an open neighborhood of θ₀, assume the common support above, fθ>0 on it, twice continuous parameter differentiability almost everywhere, and ν-integrable envelopes for each first and second derivative of fθ. Assume the score outer product and Hessian are integrable under fθ₀. Dominated differentiation may then pass through ∫fθdν=1 twice. At θ₀,

E[s]=∫(∂f/∂θ)dν=0,
H=(∂²f/∂θ∂θ′)/f−ss′,
E[H]+E[ss′]=∫(∂²f/∂θ∂θ′)dν=0.

Thus the information equality is I(θ₀)=Var(s)=E[ss′]=−E[H]. It follows from the actual normalized density and justified derivatives. It is not merely a convention for labeling an estimated Hessian. The same argument can be made conditional on X under suitable conditional domination; it then gives E[s|X]=0.

Under misspecification retain two matrices: A=−EPH(W,θ*) and B=VarPs(W,θ*). They generally differ. If an interior pseudo-target permits differentiating its population objective, its unconditional score mean is zero; that does not imply E[s|X]=0. A model-based inverse Hessian can therefore give the wrong variance even when the estimator has a well-defined, consistently estimated pseudo-target.

3. A complete regular iid argument

Global conditions. Let Wᵢ be iid, with fixed k. Let Θ⊂ℝk be nonempty and compact. Suppose ℓ(w,θ) is continuous in θ almost surely, Q(θ)=Eℓ(W,θ) is finite and continuous, and Q has a unique maximizer θ* in the interior of Θ. Assume supΘ|Qₙ−Q|→P0 and measurability of the relevant suprema. Choose a measurable exact global maximizer θ̂ of Qₙ; continuity and compactness ensure existence, while measurable selection is an explicit requirement. One sufficient iid route to uniform convergence is an integrable value at an anchor and an integrable Lipschitz envelope for ℓ on Θ, by c01's finite-net argument.

Consistency proof. For each ε>0, continuity, compactness and uniqueness give a positive gap δ between Q(θ*) and the supremum over {θ∈Θ:‖θ−θ*‖≥ε}, when that set is nonempty. On the event sup|Qₙ−Q|<δ/3, every parameter in that set has sample objective below Qₙ(θ*). A maximizer cannot lie there. The event has probability tending to one, proving θ̂→Pθ*. An objective approximation error oP(1) also suffices for consistency; it does not by itself justify the following distributional conclusion.

Local conditions. On an open ball around θ*, suppose ℓ is twice continuously differentiable, Hₙ(θ)=n−1∑H(Wᵢ,θ) converges uniformly in probability to a continuous H̄(θ), and H̄(θ*)=−A with A positive definite. Require E s(W,θ*)=0 and E‖s(W,θ*)‖²<∞; the iid CLT then gives n−1/2∑sᵢ⇒N(0,B). Differentiating Q under a dominated envelope is one way to establish the score centering at an interior maximum. It is not implied just by a numerical first-order condition.

Rate and signed expansion. Consistency and interiority place θ̂ and its segment to θ* inside that ball with probability tending to one. The sample score is then zero. By integrating the Hessian along the segment, rather than assuming one multivariate mean-value point,

0=sₙ(θ*)+H̄ₙ(θ̂−θ*),
H̄ₙ=∫₀¹Hₙ(θ*+t(θ̂−θ*))dt →P−A,
√n(θ̂−θ*)=−H̄ₙ−1n−1/2∑sᵢ
=A−1n−1/2∑sᵢ+oP(1) ⇒ N(0,A−1BA−1).

The inverse exists with probability tending to one because its limit is nonsingular. The bounded inverse and score CLT establish the root-n rate; no root-n rate was assumed to expand the equation. The positive sign uses s=∂ℓ and A=−E H. Using the gradient of the negative log likelihood instead changes both derivative conventions. An approximate score solver may use this expansion if its score residual is oP(n−1/2) and it separately satisfies the global consistency requirement. A stationary point selected far from θ* is not covered.

Feasible sandwich. Let Â=−n−1∑H(Wᵢ,θ̂) and B̂=n−1∑s(Wᵢ,θ̂)s(Wᵢ,θ̂)′. The uniform Hessian condition proves Â→PA. For B̂, add a local score Lipschitz envelope ‖s(W,θ)−s(W,θ*)‖≤L(W)‖θ−θ*‖ with E[L²]<∞. The mean squared score difference is bounded by ‖θ̂−θ*‖²n−1∑Lᵢ²=oP(1). Expanding the score outer product and bounding the two cross terms by Cauchy–Schwarz gives a vanishing difference from the true-score sample second moment. Its LLN limit is B because the true score is centered. Hence V̂=Â−1B̂Â−1 is consistent. The proof allows estimation on the same observations.

Under the correct regular likelihood, A=B=I and the covariance reduces to I−1. Otherwise use the sandwich for the stated pseudo-target. For a smooth scalar functional q, the delta-method variance is ∇q(θ*)′V∇q(θ*); for a positive limiting variance its plug-in estimate supports asymptotic studentization. Neither robust covariance nor a converged optimizer repairs an incorrectly identified target, a boundary optimum, dependence or instrument/specification selection. The M-estimation lecture supplies the general framework; the sufficient conditions above delimit the theorem used here.

Worked case 1: a rate, a mean and their units

Waiting time Y≥0, measured in hours, has density fλ(y)=λe−λy, λ>0 measured in hours−1. Its support does not depend on λ. The log density is log λ−λY, score 1/λ−Y and Hessian −1/λ². Integrating the exponential density gives E Y=1/λ and Var(Y)=1/λ², so I(λ)=1/λ² has units hours². For λ in a compact interval bounded away from zero, the derivative envelopes are integrable and the regular theorem applies when the true value is interior.

For a sample with positive sum S, the total score n/λ−S gives the unique unconstrained maximum λ̂=n/S; strict negative curvature and the decline at both endpoints establish globality. On a specified compact interval the maximizer is this value clipped to the interval. If every recorded waiting time is zero, the unconstrained likelihood has no finite maximum as λ→∞; that event has probability zero under the continuous model but must not be silently accepted by a numerical routine.

Take six original readings (1/2,1,3/2,2,5/2,3) hours. Their sum is 21/2 hours, giving λ̂=4/7 hours−1 and fitted mean 1/λ̂=7/4 hours. Plug-in information per observation is 49/16 hours² and total information is 147/8 hours². The plug-in root-n variance of λ̂ is 16/49 hours−2; its standard error is 4/(7√6)≈0.233284737 hours−1.

For the mean q(λ)=1/λ, q′=−1/λ², so the root-n variance is 1/λ² and the fitted mean's standard error is 7/(4√6) hours. For η=log λ, interpreted as the log of the numerical rate relative to one hour−1, the root-n variance is 1 and its standard error is 1/√6. These are asymptotic standard errors; six observations do not make their normal approximation exact. The population KL gap for candidate λ versus true λ₀ is log(λ₀/λ)+λ/λ₀−1, which is nonnegative by log t≤t−1.

4. Binary response: probability, coefficient and effect

For Y∈{0,1}, let x be a k×1 covariate vector, η=x′β and pβ(x)=Λ(η)=eη/(1+eη). The Bernoulli log likelihood is ℓ=Yη−log(1+eη). Differentiating Λ gives Λ′=p(1−p), hence

s=x(Y−p), H=−p(1−p)xx′.

Explicit sufficient model. Suppose observations are iid, ‖x‖≤M almost surely, Θ is compact and convex, β₀ is interior, E[xx′] is positive definite, and Y|x is Bernoulli with probability Λ(x′β₀). Bounded x and Θ bound the index, keeping fitted probabilities uniformly away from 0 and 1. Log likelihood and its needed derivatives therefore have integrable bounded envelopes. The conditional KL argument identifies β₀: equality of probabilities implies x′(β−β₀)=0 almost surely by strict monotonicity of Λ, and the positive-definite second moment then implies β=β₀. For nonzero d, E[p(1−p)(x′d)²]>0, so the information is positive definite. The regular theorem follows, and E[ss′|x]=p(1−p)xx′ directly confirms information equality.

Positive curvature does not ensure a finite unconstrained estimator in every sample. If all D=0 observations fail and all D=1 observations succeed, with x=(1,D)′, the path β(t)=(−t,2t)′ gives the correct-class probability Λ(t) for every row. Its log likelihood n log Λ(t) strictly increases to 0 as t→∞; any finite coefficient gives a negative value. No finite unconstrained maximum exists. A compact parameter domain forces an attained maximum, but it is on the boundary: at any interior point the direction (−1,2) improves the fit. Treating that boundary coefficient as an ordinary interior MLE does not follow from the theorem.

For a genuinely continuous covariate xj entering the index linearly without interactions, the fitted derivative is ∂p/∂xj=βjp(1−p). For a binary D, use the finite difference Λ(β₀+βD+w′γ)−Λ(β₀+w′γ). Interactions and transformed regressors require the full chain rule. A coefficient is a log-odds change per unit, not a probability change. Its exponential is an odds ratio under this specified model.

For comparison, a probit probability p=Φ(η), with standard normal density φ, gives by the same chain rule s=xφ(η)(Y−p)/[p(1−p)], continuous derivative βjφ(η), and binary difference Φ(η+βD)−Φ(η) when other terms are fixed. These formulas derive from differentiating Y log p+(1−Y)log(1−p); they do not by themselves prove a regular estimation theorem or a latent causal interpretation. Any latent-index scale must be normalized before coefficients are identified.

Worked case 2: an exact group fit and a different probability contrast

In a population, D is Bernoulli(1/2), x=(1,D)′, and success probabilities are p₀=1/4 and p₁=3/4. The true logit coefficients are β₀=−log 3 and β₁=2 log 3. An original sample of 80 has 40 observations in each group, with 10 and 30 successes. Maximizing each group's binomial log likelihood gives its observed success fraction. Both fractions are interior, so the fitted coefficients equal the stated population values for this particular table.

Original binary sample
DObservationsSuccessesFailuresFitted probability
04010301/4
14030103/4
I=E[p(1−p)xx′]=[(3/16,3/32);(3/32,3/32)],
I−1=[(32/3,−32/3);(−32/3,64/3)],
Cov̂(β̂)=I−1/80=[(2/15,−2/15);(−2/15,4/15)].

The fitted binary probability contrast is 1/2. Its gradient with respect to (β₀,β₁) is (p₁(1−p₁)−p₀(1−p₀),p₁(1−p₁))′=(0,3/16)′. The delta-method estimated variance of that contrast is 3/320, agreeing with the sum of the two independent group proportion variances conditional on these group sizes. The fitted infinitesimal derivative of the logistic interpolation at either D endpoint is 3 log 3/8≈0.411979608, not 1/2. The binary law supplies no infinitesimal movement of D: this derivative is a property of the interpolating curve, whereas the discrete contrast is evaluated at both observed support points. Neither number alone establishes a causal effect.

5. Average predictive effects have two sources of uncertainty

Let h(X,β) be a specified scalar predictive contrast or derivative, and let τ=E[h(X,β*)] under the actual covariate distribution. An estimator that averages over the same observations is τ̂=n−1∑h(Xᵢ,β̂). Even with a known β*, a random empirical distribution of X makes that average vary across samples. The predictive-effects lecture makes this distribution-estimation component explicit through stacked moments. Here we derive its signed influence directly.

Assume the regular parameter expansion √n(β̂−β*)=n−1/2∑ψᵢ+oP(1), where ψ=A−1s has mean zero and finite second moment. Suppose h is continuously differentiable locally, its sample-average gradient converges uniformly to a continuous population gradient, and h(X,β*) has finite second moment. Integrable local derivative envelopes and a finite-net LLN are sufficient for that uniform convergence. Write G=E[∇βh(X,β*)], a k×1 vector. Split the estimation error and integrate the gradient along the parameter segment:

√n(τ̂−τ)=n−1/2∑[h(Xᵢ,β*)−τ]+G′√n(β̂−β*)+oP(1)
=n−1/2∑{h(Xᵢ,β*)−τ+G′ψᵢ}+oP(1).

The joint iid CLT gives a centered normal limit with variance

Vτ=Var(h)+G′VβG+2G′Cov(ψ,h).

If E[s|X]=0, then E[(h−τ)ψ]=E[(h−τ)A−1E[s|X]]=0, so the cross term vanishes. A correct conditional likelihood gives this centering; a correctly specified conditional mean score can also give it without a correct full density. At a misspecified pseudo-target, E[s]=0 alone does not justify dropping the cross term. Exercise 7 constructs a nonzero example.

A consistent variance estimate can average squared estimated influences, using h(Xᵢ,β̂)−τ̂+Ĝ′Â−1s(Wᵢ,β̂), when the corresponding local L² envelopes and derivative convergence hold. The same squared-difference and Cauchy–Schwarz argument as in Section 3 justifies replacement. By contrast, for a known fixed target distribution M, τM(β)=∫h(x,β)dM(x) and the plug-in estimator has influence GM′ψ only. Estimating M from these observations, knowing M in advance, and reporting an effect conditional on a particular fixed covariate array are different statistical tasks.

Worked case 3: estimating both a curve and the distribution over it

Suppose X takes −1,0,1 with equal probabilities, the regressor vector is x=(1,X)′, and the correct conditional logit has β=(0,L)′ with L=log 3. The success probabilities are 1/4,1/2,3/4. Define h(X,β)=β₁p(1−p), the derivative of the fitted probability curve with respect to its scalar argument, evaluated at these support points. It is a model-dependent predictive interpolation functional: the discrete covariate law supplies no infinitesimal observed variation of X. Its interpretation is distinct from a finite binary contrast and from a causal effect.

The three h values are 3L/16,L/4,3L/16, so τ=5L/24≈0.228877560. Direct averaging gives I=diag(5/24,1/8). Since ∂h/∂β₀=β₁p(1−p)(1−2p) and ∂h/∂β₁=p(1−p)+β₁p(1−p)(1−2p)X, symmetry gives

G=(0,g)′, g=5/24−L/16,
Var(h)=L²/1152, G′I−1G=8g²,
Vτ=L²/1152+8(5/24−L/16)²≈0.157109516.

The cross covariance is zero here because the conditional score is centered, not because averaging and parameter estimation used separate samples. At n=300 the population-scale asymptotic standard error is approximately 0.022884457. These are calculations under the stipulated iid law, not results from an actual 300-row dataset. If the equal-probability target distribution were known and integrated exactly, only 8g² would appear. Silently treating an estimated target distribution as known drops the L²/1152 term.

6. Poisson mean models and robust quasi-likelihood

A Poisson conditional law with mean μ(x)=exp(x′β) assigns mass exp(−μ)μY/Y! to nonnegative integer Y. Omitting the parameter-free term −log(Y!), the criterion is q(Y,x;β)=Yx′β−exp(x′β). Its score is s=x(Y−μ), and its Hessian is −μxx′. The equality Var(Y|x)=μ belongs to the Poisson distribution; it is not required just to center this score.

A sufficient correct-mean theorem. Let (Y,x) be iid, Y a nonnegative integer with E[Y²]<∞, ‖x‖≤M, E[xx′] positive definite, and Θ compact and convex with β₀ interior. Suppose only E[Y|x]=μ₀(x)=exp(x′β₀). For t=x′(β−β₀), conditional averaging yields

E[q(β)−q(β₀)|x]=−μ₀(x)[et−1−t]≤0.

Since et≥1+t with equality only at t=0, equality in the unconditional objective requires x′(β−β₀)=0 almost surely; rank then gives β=β₀. This proves global identification for the mean criterion. Its Lipschitz envelope is bounded by M(Y+C) for finite C on the compact index range, so the uniform LLN follows from integrability. The score has a finite second moment, the Hessian and its parameter derivative are bounded, and A=E[μ₀xx′] is positive definite. All conditions of the regular theorem and feasible-score replacement therefore hold. A measurable global maximizer over Θ is consistent, and

√n(β̂−β₀)⇒N(0,A−1BA−1),
A=E[μ₀xx′], B=E[Var(Y|x)xx′].

The last expression uses E[Y−μ₀|x]=0. A Poisson law makes B=A; other correct-mean laws need not. The sample sandwich uses Â=n−1∑μ̂ᵢxᵢxᵢ′ and B̂=n−1∑(Yᵢ−μ̂ᵢ)²xᵢxᵢ′, with covariance estimate Â−1B̂Â−1/n. A rank-deficient sample or an unconstrained zero-count group can still prevent an interior finite fit. Covariance robustness is not a theorem about all sampling schemes or all optimizers.

If the conditional mean is wrong, the estimator may converge to an interior pseudo-target satisfying E[x(Y−exp(x′β*))]=0 under suitable identification and regularity. That unconditional equation does not assert E[Y|x]=exp(x′β*) or a structural causal interpretation. Robust errors quantify sampling variation around the pseudo-target; they do not correct its mean specification. The inspected Cameron–Trivedi preprint, Section 4.1 develops the correct-mean quasi-likelihood sandwich. Its distributional and sampling qualifications matter.

For a continuous xj entering linearly, ∂μ/∂xj=βjμ. An exact one-unit increase multiplies the mean by exp(βj), so its finite difference is μ[exp(βj)−1]. A binary contrast uses the two fitted means. The derivative and the finite difference coincide only under an appropriate approximation, not as an algebraic identity.

Worked case 4: the mean is right, the Poisson variance is wrong

D is Bernoulli(1/2), x=(1,D)′. Given D=0, Y is 0 or 4 equally; given D=1, Y is 0 or 8 equally. Conditional means are 2 and 4, variances 4 and 16. Thus the exponential mean is correct at β=(log 2,log 2)′, while neither conditional distribution is Poisson. Averaging the four equally likely states gives

A=[(3,2);(2,2)], B=[(10,8);(8,8)],
Vrobust=A−1BA−1=[(2,−2);(−2,4)],
VPoisson model=A−1=[(1,−1);(−1,3/2)].

The true root-n slope variance is 4, whereas the Poisson formula gives 3/2. The parameter still targets the conditional means under the proved conditions. Inflating a confidence interval does not require changing that point-estimation criterion.

Now take a separate finite sample with four rows per group, as follows. It need not reproduce population proportions of count values.

Original count sample
DObserved countsGroup meanMean squared fitted residual
00, 0, 4, 424
10, 8, 8, 8612

The group scores set fitted means to 2 and 6, so β̂=(log 2,log 3)′. Direct row sums give Â=[(4,3);(3,3)] and B̂=[(8,6);(6,6)]. The fitted root-n sandwich is [(2,−2);(−2,8/3)], so its slope entry is 8/3; division by n=8 gives the coefficient's estimated variance 1/3. The model-only estimate gives 1/6 for that covariance entry. All finite values use residuals around the fitted means, not the population means or the linear index x′β̂. Eight rows do not establish a finite-sample normal approximation.

7. Selection changes the observed likelihood

Let D=1{a+v>0} indicate that an outcome is observed, and let the latent outcome be Y=μ+u. Conditional on given covariates, a and μ may be different indices. Assume v and e are independent standard normals, u=ρσv+σ√(1−ρ²)e, σ>0 and |ρ|<1. These are strong conditional distributional assumptions, not consequences of seeing a selected sample. For D=0 the outcome is missing. A stored zero for that missing value is not an observed outcome equal to zero.

Put t=(y−μ)/σ. Marginally t is standard normal. The orthogonal rotation t=ρv+√(1−ρ²)e and r=√(1−ρ²)v−ρe gives independent standard normals t,r, with v=ρt+√(1−ρ²)r. Conditional on t, the selection probability is therefore Φ((a+ρt)/√(1−ρ²)). Multiplying by the marginal outcome density gives the joint observed contribution

f(y,D=1)=φ(t)Φ((a+ρt)/√(1−ρ²))/σ,
P(D=0)=Φ(−a).

The density is relative to Lebesgue measure for y when D=1 and one probability-mass point for the missing outcome when D=0. Its selected part integrates to P(D=1)=Φ(a); adding the D=0 mass gives one. For a sample with both selected and unselected units, sum D log f(y,D=1)+(1−D)log Φ(−a). The selection lecture motivates this mixed observed-data factorization; the normal formula above has been derived rather than assumed.

If the sampling experiment instead conditions on selection and includes only selected units, its density is

f(y|D=1)=f(y,D=1)/Φ(a).

Dividing by Φ(a) matters when parameters determining a are estimated. Omitting it from a selected-only likelihood treats selected observations as if their sampling probability supplied additional information. Conversely, using only the conditional selected density in a joint-data likelihood discards the observed selection counts. The observation scheme determines which likelihood is correct.

Inverse Mills mean. Since φ′(v)=−vφ(v), integration gives ∫−a∞vφ(v)dv=φ(a). Define λ(a)=φ(a)/Φ(a). Independence of e from selection gives

E[Y|D=1]=μ+ρσλ(a).

The selected mean need not equal μ. Setting ρ=0 removes this disturbance-selection correlation under the stated model; it does not by itself prove that covariates are causally exogenous. An excluded covariate that shifts a but not μ may help separate selection from the outcome index, provided its exclusion and the conditional disturbance law are defensible. A normal functional form alone is not a universal identification argument: rank, support, variation and parameter restrictions still need assessment. We have proved the observed density and selected mean, not a general identification or regular-MLE theorem for every selection specification.

Worked case 5: selection probability is not a normalizing constant to discard

Take a=0, μ=10 surplus units, σ=2 units and ρ=1/2. Half the population is selected. The selected mean is 10+√(2/π)≈10.797884561, even though the unconditional latent mean is 10. The difference is induced by selection on the correlated disturbance.

At the specific outcome y=10, t=0. The joint selected density is φ(0)Φ(0)/2=1/(4√(2π))≈0.099735570 per surplus unit. The conditional density among selected units divides by 1/2, giving 1/(2√(2π))≈0.199471140 per unit. Neither density value is a point probability. Their integrals are respectively 1/2 and 1. Changing ρ to −1/2 reverses the selected-mean displacement while leaving P(D=1) unchanged. A likelihood that ignores selection can therefore mistake a sample-composition shift for a change in μ.

8. A support boundary defeats regular information reasoning

Let Yᵢ be iid Uniform[0,θ], θ>0. The density fθ(y)=θ−11{0≤y≤θ} has parameter-dependent support. At a fixed interior observation y<θ, differentiating the log density gives score −1/θ, whose expectation is also −1/θ. Normalization is not contradicted: differentiating ∫₀θθ−1dy includes both the integral derivative −1/θ and the moving-boundary contribution +1/θ. Ignoring the support indicator loses that contribution. The common-support dominated interchange from Section 2 fails.

For nonnegative observations with maximum Mₙ>0, the likelihood is θ−n1{θ≥Mₙ}. It is zero below Mₙ and strictly decreasing above it, so θ̂=Mₙ is the measurable, unique MLE. If all observations were zero, no finite positive maximizer would exist as θ↓0; that event has probability zero under the model. The true parameter is interior to (0,∞), but the sample likelihood is not regular at its support-determined optimum.

For 0≤m≤θ, independence gives P(Mₙ≤m)=(m/θ)n. Thus for fixed t≥0 and n≥t,

P(n(θ−Mₙ)/θ>t)=(1−t/n)n → e−t.

The limiting law is unit exponential, on the n scale. Hence √n(Mₙ−θ)→P0, a degenerate limit rather than the claimed regular nondegenerate information law. Direct tail integration also gives E Mₙ=nθ/(n+1). For any 0<α<1,

[Mₙ, Mₙ/α1/n]

has exactly 1−α coverage: its lower endpoint is always at most θ, and θ≤Mₙ/α1/n is equivalent to Mₙ/θ≥α1/n, an event with probability 1−α. Exact coverage here comes from the distribution of the maximum, not from a robust Hessian or a normal approximation.

Worked case 6: the maximum is informative at a different rate

Four original readings are (1,2,3,4), so M₄=4. Under a hypothetical true θ=5 in repeated samples, the mean of M₄ is 4 and the probability P(4(5−M₄)/5>1) is (3/4)⁴=81/256. Its limiting counterpart e−1 is about 0.367879; these need not agree at n=4. Taking α=1/16 makes α1/4=1/2, so the exact interval for the observed sample is [4,8] with coverage 15/16 across repetitions from any θ>0. Coverage is a property of that random procedure, not a posterior probability assigned to this fixed interval.

9. What an empirical likelihood claim must report

Define the observed unit, support, sampling mechanism, outcome scale and target before fitting. Distinguish a conditional prediction from a causal effect; a correct conditional mean from a full distribution; and a selected-only sample from observed selection indicators for everyone. State identification separately from numerical curvature. Check finite existence, parameter boundaries, rank and the actual first-order residual before invoking a local limit.

For uncertainty, name the score, curvature, covariance, sampling units and target distribution. Show why the information equality or a zero cross covariance is justified when either is used. Report finite and derivative effects with their units. A robust covariance, a held-out predictive score and a successfully converged optimizer address different questions; none independently validates exclusion, selection assumptions or an intervention claim.

The companion readonly checker reconstructs these finite distributions and sample scores, matrix covariances, average-effect influences, selection integrals and boundary probabilities using the standard library. Numerical evidence checks examples and meaningful altered assumptions. The analytic proofs establish the stated general claims; finite checks do not substitute for them or establish empirical validity.

Exercises: prove, calculate and diagnose

Specify the target, observation scheme, parameter domain, units and sampling assumptions. Separate exact algebra from an asymptotic calibration. In the open audit, justified alternative designs earn credit; an unsupported preferred conclusion does not.

  1. Under Section 1's common-support and integrability assumptions, prove the population KL identity and its equality condition. Explain why equal densities do not imply equal parameter labels without identification. Extend the argument to conditional likelihood, and explain why maximizing an expected working likelihood need not identify a causal parameter.
  2. Derive the exponential likelihood, score, information and unrestricted MLE, including its existence exception. For worked case 1, convert every waiting time from hours to minutes and calculate the new rate, mean, one-observation information and rate standard error. Explain why the log-rate standard error is unchanged, and why the mean and rate variances transform differently.
  3. Prove the regular iid consistency and root-n expansion from Section 3 without assuming the root-n rate. State the uniform/global, interior, Hessian, score and measurable-selection conditions. Derive the sandwich sign and the score-covariance replacement bound. Explain separately what an oP(1) objective error and an oP(n−1/2) score residual establish.
  4. A new binary sample has 20 observations per D group, with 4 successes when D=0 and 16 when D=1. Fit the intercept-and-D logit, calculate the odds ratio and discrete probability contrast, and compute the plug-in information, coefficient covariance and delta variance of that contrast using the balanced empirical covariate distribution. Give an independent group-proportion check and state the inference limitation.
  5. For the perfectly separated binary sample described in Section 4, prove nonexistence of a finite unconstrained MLE. In the restricted path β(t)=(−t,2t)′, t∈[0,2], locate the optimum and explain why a zero-score interior theorem does not apply. Separately derive the probit score and continuous covariate derivative. At index zero, calculate the intercept score for Y=1 and the fitted continuous derivative when that covariate coefficient equals 2.
  6. Derive the influence of an average predictive functional that estimates its covariate distribution from the same observations. State sufficient regularity and the cross-covariance condition. Reproduce every component of worked case 3's variance, and explain how the answer changes if the equal-probability target distribution is known and integrated exactly.
  7. Let a known offset X be 0 or log 3 equally often in the iid population. The actual conditional Y distribution is Bernoulli(5/8) at both X values. Fit the working probability pβ(X)=Λ(β+X), estimating only the intercept β over a compact interval containing 0 in its interior. Define h=pβ(1−pβ), the derivative of that working curve with respect to the offset, and estimate its population average by the same-sample average. Prove the unique pseudo-target is β*=0. Find A, B, τ, G, Var(h), Cov(h,s), the full influence variance, and the value obtained by wrongly discarding the cross term. Compare a known fixed target distribution and explain what the supplied discrete law does and does not identify about an actual conditional-mean derivative.
  8. Prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the bounded-regressor correct-mean Poisson quasi-likelihood under Section 6's conditions, without assuming a Poisson conditional distribution. Derive its feasible covariance. Recompute A, B and the population sandwich in worked case 4, then separately recompute the eight-row sample's fitted means, curvature, meat and slope covariance. Explain why x′β̂ is the wrong fitted value for its residual.
  9. Keep worked case 4's four-state population, but fit an intercept-only exponential mean, omitting D. Find its pseudo-target, curvature, score variance, robust root-n variance and Poisson-model variance. Calculate the conditional residual means at D=0 and D=1. Does a robust standard error recover the omitted binary contrast?
  10. Derive the observed Gaussian-selection density and the selected-only normalization from the independent v,e construction. Derive the selected mean by tail integration. Then derive Var(Y|D=1) by integrating the second moment of v above −a. Evaluate that variance at worked case 5's parameters and explain the effects of ρ=0 and ρ=−1/2 on selection probability and selected mean. Identify the additional assumptions needed before fitting this density could be given a structural interpretation.
  11. For Uniform[0,θ], prove the MLE, its exact distribution, E Mₙ, the n-rate exponential limit, and the exact [Mₙ,Mₙ/α1/n] coverage statement. Explain precisely why the ordinary score-normalization argument fails although θ is interior to (0,∞). Recompute worked case 6's finite tail and interval rather than substituting the limiting tail.
  12. An analyst says: “Our optimizer converged, so our selected-only normal model is identified. We can omit selection probabilities, use the inverse Hessian for any fitted likelihood, and interpret every logit coefficient as a causal probability change. Averaging fitted effects adds no sampling uncertainty. A maximum-based support estimate also has the usual root-n normal law. All checks run, so these conclusions are verified.” Write a research-review response with at least six distinct diagnoses. For each give the failed assumption or changed target, a defensible repair and the evidence still needed. Do not assert that one alternative model is automatically true.

Solutions and proof checks

Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Let r=fθ/fθ₀. Common normalized support gives Eθ₀r=1. The difference in expected log densities is −E log r=E[r−1−log r]≥0. The integrability assumptions allow these expectations and subtraction. Since r−1−log r is nonnegative and zero only at r=1, equality holds exactly when fθ=fθ₀ almost everywhere. A family parametrized redundantly, such as fθ depending only on θ² over positive and negative θ, can have identical densities with different labels. Injectivity at the target must be established separately.

    For a conditional model, integrate the nonnegative conditional KL gap over X. Equality means equality of conditional densities for almost every covariate value under its actual law. Covariate values absent from that law supply no additional identification. Under a misspecified family the expected criterion defines an approximation target; it need not equal a structural parameter. Even a correct conditional density does not equate a conditional comparison with an intervention without a design and assumptions linking the two.

  2. For n nonnegative times, L(λ)=λⁿexp(−λS). If S>0, the log derivative n/λ−S crosses zero at n/S and its derivative is −n/λ²<0. Log likelihood tends to −∞ as λ↓0 or λ→∞, so this is the unique global maximum. If S=0, it grows without bound as λ→∞. The one-observation score 1/λ−Y is centered because E Y=1/λ; its variance and negative expected Hessian are both 1/λ². A compact domain clips n/S and can force a boundary solution.

    The minute readings are (30,60,90,120,150,180), sum 630. The fitted rate becomes 1/105 minute−1; the mean becomes 105 minutes. Per-observation information is 11025 minutes² and the rate standard error is 1/(105√6) minute−1. The rate is divided by 60 and its variance by 60²; the mean and its standard error multiply by 60, and its variance by 60². Log rate changes by the deterministic constant −log 60, so its standard error stays 1/√6. These are transformed asymptotic standard errors, not an exact normal finite-sample result.

  3. Assume iid fixed-dimensional observations; compact Θ; almost-sure criterion continuity; finite continuous population objective with a unique interior maximum; a measurable exact global sample maximizer; measurable suprema; and uniform criterion convergence. For any ε, compact separation supplies δ>0 outside its ε-ball. Uniform error less than δ/3 makes the population maximizer beat every point outside the ball in the sample, proving consistency. An oP(1) objective error leaves the same separation argument valid after reserving part of the gap.

    On a differentiability ball, require uniform Hessian convergence to continuous H̄ with H̄(θ*)=−A, A positive definite, centered finite-variance score and its iid CLT. Consistency and interiority imply a zero sample score with probability tending to one. Integration on the segment gives 0=sₙ(θ*)+H̄ₙ(θ̂−θ*), with H̄ₙ→−A. Inverse continuity yields √n(θ̂−θ*)=A−1n−1/2∑sᵢ+oP(1). This both proves the rate and gives covariance A−1BA−1. The sign is positive because the score differentiates the log likelihood and A is the negative expected Hessian. Information equality requires its separate correct-density and interchange proof.

    For feasibility let dᵢ=s(Wᵢ,θ̂)−s(Wᵢ,θ*). A local square-integrable Lipschitz envelope gives n−1∑‖dᵢ‖²≤‖θ̂−θ*‖²n−1∑Lᵢ²=oP(1). The average outer-product difference is bounded by this quantity plus twice its square root times the square root of the average true-score squared norm. Cauchy–Schwarz and LLN make it vanish; the true-score outer product has mean B. Uniform Hessian convergence similarly gives Â→A. An approximate score residual oP(n−1/2) adds oP(1) after scaling, provided consistency is already proved. Neither a small score at an arbitrary local point nor an oP(1) objective gap alone establishes all these rate hypotheses.

  4. The group fits are p̂₀=1/5 and p̂₁=4/5. Thus β̂=(−log 4,2 log 4)′, odds ratio exp(β̂₁)=16, and discrete probability contrast 3/5. Interior group proportions and a full-rank two-group design yield a finite unique coefficient. The common fitted Bernoulli variance is 4/25, giving Î=[(4/25,2/25);(2/25,2/25)] and Î−1=[(25/2,−25/2);(−25/2,25)]. Division by 40 gives coefficient covariance [(5/16,−5/16);(−5/16,5/8)].

    The contrast gradient is (0,4/25)′, so its estimated variance is (4/25)²(5/8)=2/125. Separately, conditional on the group sizes, the sum of the two binomial proportion variances is (4/25)/20+(4/25)/20=2/125. The equality verifies the delta calculation at these fitted values. It does not make estimated-parameter normal confidence statements exact, or establish causality or the sampling assumptions from the table alone.

  5. Along β(t)=(−t,2t)′, every observed outcome in the separated sample has probability Λ(t). The log likelihood is n log Λ(t), with derivative n[1−Λ(t)]>0 for every finite t. It tends to 0 as t→∞; all finite coefficients give a negative log likelihood. Hence the supremum is not attained in the unrestricted model. Restricting this path to [0,2] yields t̂=2, where the derivative remains positive. This constrained maximum satisfies a boundary condition, not the interior zero-score equation. Compactness ensures attainment here but does not supply the missing regular interior hypothesis.

    For probit, ∂p/∂β=φ(η)x and ∂ℓ/∂p=Y/p−(1−Y)/(1−p)=(Y−p)/[p(1−p)]. Multiplication yields the stated score. Differentiating p with respect to a continuous index covariate gives βjφ(η). At η=0, p=1/2. The intercept score for Y=1 is 2φ(0)=√(2/π), and with βj=2 the fitted derivative is the same numerical value √(2/π). These two equal values have different roles and potentially different units; neither is a binary probability contrast.

  6. Write τ̂−τ=(Eₙ−E)h(X,β*)+Eₙ[h(X,β̂)−h(X,β*)]. Continuous local differentiation and uniform convergence of its sample-average gradient give the second term G′(β̂−β*)+oP(n−1/2), using the already established parameter rate. A joint finite-second-moment CLT then gives influence h−τ+G′ψ. Its variance expands into Var(h)+G′VβG+2G′Cov(ψ,h). Correct conditional score centering makes the last covariance zero by iterated expectation; unconditional centering alone does not. Local L² replacement bounds are needed for a plug-in influence variance estimate.

    For the three-point law, p=(1/4,1/2,3/4), w=p(1−p)=(3/16,1/4,3/16) and h=Lw. Thus τ=5L/24, deviations in h are (−L/48,L/24,−L/48), and their mean square is L²/1152. Averaging wxx′ gives I=diag(5/24,1/8). Differentiating h gives first gradient component with cancelling endpoint terms and second component 5/24−L/16. Hence the coefficient contribution is 8(5/24−L/16)². Adding the empirical-X term yields the worked variance. If the target distribution is fixed and known, τM(β̂) integrates the fitted curve using exact weights 1/3; its influence omits h−τ, and only the coefficient contribution remains. The derivative is still a model-dependent interpolation functional on this discrete support.

  7. At β=0, fitted probabilities are (1/2,3/4), while the actual probability is q=5/8 at both offsets. Conditional score means q−p are (1/8,−1/8), so the unconditional score is zero. The population second derivative is −E[p(1−p)]<0 for every finite β. The compact domain contains 0 in its interior, making 0 its unique global pseudo-target. No correct conditional likelihood has been asserted.

    At that target h=(1/4,3/16), giving τ=A=7/32. The derivative h′=p(1−p)(1−2p) averages to G=−3/64. For either offset, E[(Y−p)²|X]=q(1−q)+(q−p)²=15/64+1/64=1/4, so B=1/4. Deviations h−τ are (1/32,−1/32); therefore Var(h)=1/1024 and Cov(h,s)=E[(h−τ)(q−p)]=1/256. Since G/A=−3/14, the full influence is h−τ−3s/14, with

    V=1/1024+9/784−3/1792=541/50176.

    Discarding the cross term instead gives 625/50176. With the target distribution known and integrated exactly the variance is only 9/784. At the two support points the actual conditional mean equals 5/8. This discrete law does not identify a unique infinitesimal derivative: a constant extension has derivative zero, while other extensions can match both values with different derivatives. The positive average 7/32 is the defined working-logistic functional, not a recovered actual response or causal effect. A robust parameter sandwich alone would also omit its empirical-distribution and cross terms.

  8. Conditional expected criterion loss relative to β₀ is μ₀[et−1−t] with t=x′(β−β₀). It is nonnegative and vanishes only when t=0 almost surely. Positive-definite E[xx′] makes the target unique. Bounded regressors and compact Θ bound μ; the criterion has an integrable Lipschitz envelope proportional to Y+C, its score has a finite second moment because E[Y²]<∞, and its Hessian and local Hessian derivative are bounded. Uniform criterion/Hessian convergence, consistency and the score CLT therefore hold. Positive-definite A=E[μ₀xx′] permits the same signed score expansion. Conditional score centering gives B=E[Var(Y|x)xx′], with no requirement Var(Y|x)=μ₀. The feasible meat averages (Y−μ̂)²xx′ and its replacement follows from bounded-x mean Lipschitz control and the score second moment.

    For the population, each D has weight 1/2. The weighted means 2 and 4 give A=[(3,2);(2,2)]; variances 4 and 16 give B=[(10,8);(8,8)]. Inverting A gives [(1,−1);(−1,3/2)]; multiplying on both sides of B gives [(2,−2);(−2,4)]. These are root-n covariance matrices. For the eight-row table the fitted means are 2 and 6. Mean squared residuals are 4 and 12, so Â=[(4,3);(3,3)], B̂=[(8,6);(6,6)]. Here Â−1=[(1,−1);(−1,4/3)] and the root-n sandwich is [(2,−2);(−2,8/3)]. Its slope covariance is (8/3)/8=1/3. The sample and population calculations use different means and are not interchangeable. The linear index is log μ̂; residuals in this score subtract μ̂=exp(x′β̂), in count units.

  9. The unconditional mean is (2+4)/2=3, so the intercept-only population score E[Y−exp(β)] vanishes uniquely at β*=log 3. The curvature is A=3. By total variance, Var(Y)=E Var(Y|D)+Var(E[Y|D])=(4+16)/2+1=11. Thus the robust root-n variance is 11/9, while the Poisson-model value is 1/3. Conditional residual means are −1 and +1 despite their unconditional mean being zero.

    The fitted intercept-only curve predicts 3 in both D groups, hence a fitted binary contrast of zero; the actual mean contrast is 4−2=2. Robust covariance describes estimation uncertainty around log 3 in the restricted model. It neither adds the omitted regressor nor restores the missing conditional response. The correctly specified richer mean model and the misspecified intercept-only model have different targets.

  10. Write t=ρv+√(1−ρ²)e and r=√(1−ρ²)v−ρe. Orthogonality makes (t,r) independent standard normals, so conditional on t, v=ρt+√(1−ρ²)r. The selection probability at outcome y is Φ((a+ρt)/√(1−ρ²)); multiplication by φ(t)/σ gives the joint selected density. Total probability makes its integral Φ(a), while the unselected contribution is Φ(−a). Conditioning on selection therefore divides the selected density by Φ(a). Using the wrong factor changes the likelihood for its declared sampling experiment.

    Tail integration gives ∫−a∞vφ(v)dv=φ(a), so E[v|D=1]=λ(a). Integrating v²φ(v)=φ(v)−[vφ(v)]′ gives ∫−a∞v²φ(v)dv=Φ(a)−aφ(a), and hence Var(v|D=1)=1−aλ−λ². The independent e component retains variance one. Therefore

    Var(Y|D=1)=σ²[1−ρ²λ(a)(a+λ(a))].

    At a=0, σ=2, ρ=1/2 this is 4−2/π≈3.363380228. With ρ=0 the selected mean is μ and conditional variance σ²; with ρ=−1/2 the mean is 10−√(2/π), and its variance is unchanged because it depends on ρ². Selection probability is 1/2 in all three cases because it depends on a, not ρ. Structural interpretation still needs a justified covariate/assignment structure, outcome and selection exclusions, conditional joint-normal or alternative distributional assumptions, support/rank and an identified parameterization. The derived density does not establish those empirical claims.

  11. For a sample with Mₙ>0, θ<Mₙ has likelihood zero; on θ≥Mₙ the likelihood θ−n strictly decreases. Thus θ̂=Mₙ. Independence gives FM(m)=(m/θ)ⁿ on [0,θ]. Its expectation is ∫₀θ[1−(m/θ)ⁿ]dm=nθ/(n+1). For 0≤t≤n, P(n(θ−Mₙ)/θ>t)=(1−t/n)ⁿ; for t>n it is zero. Taking n→∞ at fixed t≥0 gives the unit-exponential survival function. Tightness of this normalized gap implies √n(Mₙ−θ)→0.

    The interval contains θ exactly when Mₙ/θ≥α1/n, because Mₙ≤θ already. Its complement has probability α, proving exact coverage. At n=4,t=1 the finite tail is 81/256, not e−1. For M₄=4 and α=1/16 the interval is [4,8] with 15/16 coverage. The formal interior-observation score is −1/θ and is not centered. The derivative of ∫₀θθ−1dy includes a +1/θ boundary term that cancels the integral derivative. Parameter-dependent support and nonregular sample likelihood invalidate the interchange; interiority of the true parameter alone does not repair it.

  12. Evaluation criteria. A complete response diagnoses at least six distinct claims, connects each to a target or assumption, proposes a repair and names evidence still needed. One defensible response is:

    (1) Optimizer convergence establishes neither global selection nor identification. Inspect objective/rank and existence, show an identifying argument, and distinguish an interior optimum from a compact boundary solution. (2) A selected-only density requires division by its selection probability; a joint sample instead needs both selection mass and selected density. Document who enters the dataset and retain missingness indicators. (3) Inverse Hessian covariance requires information equality under the actual likelihood and its interchange conditions. Under a justified pseudo-target use the correctly scaled score sandwich and establish sampling-unit assumptions. (4) A logit coefficient is a log-odds parameter; compute the defined discrete probability contrast or continuous derivative, with interactions and units. A causal label additionally requires a design or substantive identification assumptions. (5) An empirically averaged effect includes the covariate-distribution term. Under misspecification retain its cross covariance with coefficient influence; state whether the target distribution is known or estimated. (6) A support maximum has an n-rate exponential gap law in the proved uniform model; use its exact distribution rather than regular root-n information. (7) Executed code can check contracts and arithmetic but cannot authenticate normal selection errors, exclusion, sampling independence or external validity.

    Alternative models, sensitivity analyses, better observation records or a new research design can be legitimate repairs if their assumptions and remaining limits are explicit. Full credit requires explaining what an output does establish as well as what additional evidence it lacks. Merely replacing all formulas with the word “robust,” or asserting that a preferred estimator is causal, does not meet the criterion.

Teach-back and delayed transfer

Teach-back. In five minutes, explain to a technically trained colleague why “the model converged and the Hessian is invertible” is insufficient for a likelihood-based causal claim and standard error. Use one regular model, one misspecified-mean example, one selected-data likelihood and the moving-support counterexample. State the target before each formula.

Teach-back benchmark

A successful explanation begins with the observed-data law and target. Under a correct regular likelihood, common support and dominated differentiation center the score and equate its covariance to negative expected Hessian. Compact global selection and uniform convergence establish consistency before the local score expansion supplies the rate. Under a correct-mean Poisson criterion, the coefficient can still target that mean while its covariance needs a sandwich; an omitted conditional-mean variable instead changes the target. A predictive probability contrast is not causal without a separate design. An average over estimated covariates has an empirical-distribution influence and possibly a cross covariance. Selected-only and joint-data likelihoods have different normalization factors. Finally, a uniform endpoint is estimated by a maximum with an n-rate law, so even an interior parameter value cannot rescue regular information reasoning. A listener should be able to name which assumption, rather than which software option, licenses each step.

Delayed check. After a week without the worked cases: (i) derive the root-n variance of an intercept-only logit at p=1/3 and of h=p(1−p); (ii) for a correct intercept count mean 3 with Y∈{0,6} equally, compare robust and Poisson-model root-n variances of the log mean; (iii) in the selection construction use a=0,μ=2,σ=4,ρ=−1/4 and find the selected mean; (iv) for a uniform sample with n=2 and maximum 3, form the exact interval with α=1/9. Explain one condition that would invalidate each calculation.

Retention solution and repair route

(i) The coefficient is log[(1/3)/(2/3)]=−log 2. Information is 2/9, so root-n coefficient variance is 9/2. The derivative of h with respect to the intercept is p(1−p)(1−2p)=2/27; its root-n variance is 2/81. There is no empirical-X term in this intercept-only functional. Dependence or a constrained boundary fit would require a new argument. (ii) Var(Y)=9, giving robust log-mean variance 9/3²=1, versus model value 1/3. Wrong mean specification or infinite score variance would invalidate the stated theorem. (iii) The displacement is ρσ√(2/π)=−√(2/π), so the selected mean is 2−√(2/π); abandoning the stipulated joint-normal selection law removes this formula's justification. (iv) α1/2=1/3 gives [3,9] with 8/9 coverage. Nonuniform or dependent observations would change the maximum's distribution. Repair a score/information error in Sections 2–3, a coefficient/effect error in Sections 4–5, a mean/variance error in Section 6, an observation-scheme error in Section 7, and a rate/coverage error in Section 8. Repeat one altered numerical case and explain its assumptions aloud before advancing.

Sources, scope and next steps

Four bounded primary scopes inform the methods: Rigollet's 2016 likelihood lectures for the likelihood/KL and regular-information framework; Chernozhukov and Fernández-Val's 2017 nonlinear regression lecture for binary models, predictive effects and M-estimation; Cameron and Trivedi's June 1999 count-data preprint for mean-model quasi-likelihood; and Chernozhukov's 2007 nonlinear econometrics overview for the mixed selected-data likelihood. The source record identifies actual pages inspected and formula cautions. The finite examples, proof organization, prompts and solutions are original.

The regular results are fixed-dimensional and iid with the stated envelopes, rank, support, selection and interiority conditions. No general theorem for every nonlinear optimizer, dependent or clustered data, many parameters, model selection or causal transport has been proved. Selection inference requires additional identification and regularity beyond the density derivation. Flexible links, semiparametric selection, bootstrap validity and uniform treatment-effect inference are deeper extensions, not claims hidden inside a standard-error formula. The next chapter develops identification from repeated observations on the same units, including correlated heterogeneity, dynamic panels, attrition and within-unit dependence.

Sources and further study

  • Nonlinear and Binary Regression, Predictive Effects, and M-Estimation — Predictive/discrete and derivative effects, empirical target-distribution uncertainty, stacked moments, binary links, conditional likelihood, M-estimation and robust covariance. Empirical figures encountered are not adopted as evidence; sorted-effect/bootstrap and application results are outside chapter proof scope.
  • 14.385 Nonlinear Econometrics, Lecture1: Basic Overview of Some Principal Methods — Conditional/marginal likelihood distinction, censored mixed likelihood and the TypeII sample-selection observed-data factorization. The explicit bivariate-normal selected density and Mills mean are derived in the chapter; page14 leaves the details to homework.
  • 18.650 Statistics for Applications, Chapter 3: Maximum Likelihood Estimation — KL definition and information inequality, likelihood maximization, gradient/Hessian, examples, information and regular limit statement. PDF page numbers differ from the slide footers by one.
  • Essentials of Count Data Regression — Poisson score/mean link and interpretation, overdispersion, selected/truncated count caution and Section4.1 correct-mean quasi-likelihood sandwich. The file name contains E01 but the document title page is dated June30,1999; no final publication year is invented.
